How we won, last Onam

Every petal tells a story — here is how eleven people turned crushed marigolds into a winning pookalam.

We started three days before judging with eleven people, a WhatsApp group, and no flowers ordered yet. The rain didnt help. Half our marigold order arrived crushed, and we spent the morning of the competition re-sorting petals by hand on someone's terrace.

What got us through wasn't planning — it was that everyone who could spare an hour, gave one. Students came between classes. Aunties who said they'd "just watch" ended up laying half the outer ring. By evening the ring was seven layers deep, colour bleeding out from the centre like it had always been there.

"We didn't win because our pookalam was the biggest. We won because it had more hands in it than anyone else's."

That's the part we want to repeat this year — not just the size, the number of people who can point at a petal and say, I placed that one.

This year, more hands, more flowers

We're opening it up wider — you don't need experience, just an hour or two to spare over Onam week.

Whatever you're free for, there's a place in it:

  • Laying flowers — no design experience needed
  • Sourcing and sorting — prep the day before
  • Spreading the word — building momentum
  • Contributing — chipping in for flowers
Thank you — we'll message you on WhatsApp.

Chip in for the flowers

Marigold, jasmine, banana leaves, and colour powders add up fast — ₹50 or whatever you can spare goes straight into this year's pookalam.

Everyone who contributes gets a small thank-you:

White mullapoo, for girls and women who give

A strand of fresh jasmine to wear, ready for you to collect on judging day.
